intro.title: Opening and reading files
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Everything a program has stored in variables disappears when it ends. **Files** keep data for later: notes, settings, scores, logs, whole books. This quest is about reading and writing them.

In CodeQuest, Python runs in your browser with a small disk of its own. Files you create in the sandbox stay there until the page reloads (or a run is stopped), and every challenge check starts in a fresh, empty folder, with the sample files that challenge needs already in it.

`open(name)` opens a file and gives you a **file object**. Its `read()` method returns the whole content as one string, and `close()` tells Python you've finished with it. The example first creates a small file to read; writing files gets its own stage soon.

```
f = open("hello.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8")    # create a file to read
f.write("Hello, file!\nSecond line\n")
f.close()

f = open("hello.txt", encoding="utf-8")
text = f.read()
f.close()
print(text)
```

The second argument of `open` is the **mode**: `"r"` to read (the default), `"w"` to write. Pass `encoding="utf-8"` as well, so that letters like é and ø are read correctly whatever computer the file came from; the stage on bytes explains why.

The text you get back includes the line breaks, as `\n` characters. `text.splitlines()` turns it into a list of lines without them, and `len(text)` counts every character, line breaks included.

A file object remembers how far it has read. After `read()` has returned everything, a second `read()` returns `""`, because there's nothing left. `read(5)` reads at most 5 characters, and the next read carries on from there.

```
f = open("hello.txt", encoding="utf-8")
print(repr(f.read(5)))    # 'Hello'
print(repr(f.read(2)))    # ', '
rest = f.read()
print(repr(f.read()))     # '' : nothing left
f.close()
```

Opening a file that doesn't exist raises `FileNotFoundError`. And forgetting `close()` can leave files locked or half-written in real programs, which is why the next stage shows the `with` statement, which closes files for you.

intro.title: The with statement
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Remembering to call `close()` is easy to forget, and if an error happens between `open` and `close`, the `close()` line never runs. The `with` statement solves both problems: it opens the file, runs the indented block, and **always** closes the file afterwards, whether the block finished normally or with an error.

```
with open("hello.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Hello again!\n")

with open("hello.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    text = f.read()

print(text)
print(f.closed)   # True: closed as soon as the block ended
```

Read it as: "with the file `hello.txt` open, and called `f`, do this". The name after `as` is the file object, just like the result of `open` in the last stage. Variables you create inside the block, such as `text`, still exist after it; only the file is closed.

From now on, use `with` whenever you open a file. It's shorter, it can't forget, and every experienced Python programmer will expect it.

One `with` can open several files at once, separated by commas, which is handy for reading one file while writing another:

```
with open("a.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("from a\n")

with open("a.txt", encoding="utf-8") as src, open("b.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as dst:
    dst.write(src.read().upper())
```

Wrapping the `with` in a function gives you a small, reusable tool: `read_file(name)` that returns the text, or `count_lines(name)`. The file is opened and closed inside, and the caller never has to think about it.

`with` isn't only for files. It works with anything that needs setting up and tidying away, such as network connections and locks. Objects that work with `with` are called **context managers**.

intro.title: Reading line by line
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`read()` loads the whole file at once, which is fine for small files. Most of the time, though, you want to work through a file **one line at a time**, and a file object lets you loop over it directly:

```
with open("poem.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Roses are red\nViolets are blue\n")

with open("poem.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(repr(line))     # 'Roses are red\n', then 'Violets are blue\n'
```

Each line still ends with its `\n`. Printing it as it is gives you an extra blank line, so take it off first: `line.rstrip("\n")` removes just the line break, and `line.strip()` removes spaces at both ends too. The last line of a file may or may not end with `\n`, and stripping handles both.

Looping over the file is also the **memory-friendly** way: Python reads one line, hands it to you, and forgets it, so even a file of several gigabytes works. `read()` or `readlines()` would load all of it at once.

`enumerate(f, start=1)` numbers the lines as you go, which is handy for messages like "line 7 is broken". Inside the loop, skip what you don't want with `continue`: blank lines (`if not line.strip():`) or comments (`if line.startswith("#"):`).

```
with open("data.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("# scores\nAna,91\n\nBen,78\n")

scores = {}
with open("data.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for number, line in enumerate(f, start=1):
        line = line.strip()
        if not line or line.startswith("#"):
            continue
        name, score = line.split(",")
        scores[name] = int(score)
print(scores)   # {'Ana': 91, 'Ben': 78}
```

Two other methods: `f.readline()` reads just the next line (`""` at the end of the file), useful for a header line before looping over the rest; and `f.readlines()` returns a list of all the lines, `\n` included. To get the lines without their breaks, `f.read().splitlines()` is usually neater.

A file object can only be looped over **once**: a second loop starts where the first finished, at the end, and finds nothing. Open the file again, or keep the lines you need in a list.

intro.title: Writing files
intro.bodyMarkdown:
To write a file, open it in mode `"w"` and call `write` with the text. If the file doesn't exist it's created; if it **does** exist, everything in it is thrown away first. `"w"` always starts from an empty file, so be sure you mean it.

```
with open("greeting.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Hello!\n")
    f.write("This is line two.\n")

with open("greeting.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())
```

`write` writes exactly what you give it and nothing more: no space, and **no line break** at the end. Add `"\n"` yourself wherever a line should end, or the lines will run together. It also only takes strings, so numbers need `str()` or an f-string first: `f.write(f"{score}\n")`.

`print` can write to a file too, with `file=f`. It works just like printing to the screen: it converts values to text, puts spaces between them and adds the line break for you, so it's often the most convenient way to write lines.

```
scores = {"Ana": 91, "Ben": 78}
with open("scores.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for name, score in scores.items():
        print(name, score, sep=": ", file=f)

with open("scores.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())   # Ana: 91, then Ben: 78
```

To write many lines at once, join them: `f.write("\n".join(lines) + "\n")`. (There's also `f.writelines(lines)`, which, despite its name, adds no line breaks either.)

Written text may sit in a buffer for a moment before it reaches the file. Closing the file (which `with` does for you) makes sure everything is written. Don't read a file back while you still have it open for writing; let the `with` block end first.

A common pattern is **read, change, write**: read a file, transform its contents, and write the result to a new file. Writing to a **different** name keeps the original safe if something goes wrong halfway.

intro.title: Appending and file modes
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Mode `"w"` replaces a file. Often you want to **add** to it instead: another line in a diary, another entry in a log. Mode `"a"` (append) opens the file and writes at the end, keeping everything already there. Like `"w"`, it creates the file if it doesn't exist.

```
with open("diary.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Monday: rain\n")

with open("diary.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Tuesday: sun\n")

with open("diary.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())   # both days are there
```

Appended text goes right after the last character in the file. If the file doesn't end with a line break, the new text joins the last line, so programs that append usually write a full line each time, ending with `\n`.

The modes you'll use most:

```
"r"    read (the default); the file must exist
"w"    write; creates the file, or empties an existing one
"a"    append; creates the file, or adds to the end
"x"    create; fails with FileExistsError if the file exists
"r+"   read and write an existing file, from the start
```

`"x"` is the safe choice when you must not overwrite anything, such as a new save file or an exported report: it raises `FileExistsError` instead of quietly destroying an existing file. Add `b` to any mode for binary files (`"rb"`, `"wb"`), which the stage on bytes covers.

A file that's both read and updated, like a counter or a list of unique entries, is usually easiest to handle in two steps: read the whole thing, work out the new content, then write it back with `"w"` (or append just the new part with `"a"`).

```
def add_unique(name, item):
    try:
        with open(name, encoding="utf-8") as f:
            existing = f.read().splitlines()
    except FileNotFoundError:     # no file yet: nothing in it
        existing = []
    if item not in existing:
        with open(name, "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            f.write(item + "\n")

add_unique("tags.txt", "python")
add_unique("tags.txt", "python")   # already there: nothing added
```

intro.title: Paths and folders
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A file name like `"notes.txt"` is a **relative path**: Python looks for it in the **current working directory**, the folder the program is running in, which `os.getcwd()` shows. A path that starts from the top of the disk, like `/home/ana/notes.txt` (or `C:\Users\Ana\notes.txt` on Windows), is an **absolute path** and means the same file wherever the program runs.

The `os` module (`import os`) works with paths and folders. Folders are separated by `/` on Mac and Linux and by `\` on Windows, so instead of gluing strings together, build paths with `os.path.join`, which uses the right separator for the computer it runs on:

```
import os

path = os.path.join("data", "2026", "sales.txt")
print(path)                          # data/2026/sales.txt on Mac and Linux
print(os.path.basename(path))        # sales.txt
print(os.path.dirname(path))         # data/2026
print(os.path.splitext(path))        # ('data/2026/sales', '.txt')
```

These functions only work with the **text** of a path; the file doesn't need to exist. To ask about the disk, use `os.path.exists(path)`, `os.path.isfile(path)` and `os.path.isdir(path)`, which return `True` or `False`, and `os.path.getsize(path)` for a file's size in bytes.

`os.makedirs("data/2026", exist_ok=True)` creates a folder, including any missing folders above it; `exist_ok=True` means "and don't complain if it's already there". `os.listdir(folder)` returns the names of everything in a folder, files and folders alike, in no particular order, so sort them when the order matters.

```
import os

os.makedirs("reports", exist_ok=True)
with open(os.path.join("reports", "jan.txt"), "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("January\n")
print(sorted(os.listdir("reports")))       # ['jan.txt']
print(os.path.exists("reports/jan.txt"))   # True
```

`os.rename(old, new)` renames or moves a file, and `os.remove(path)` deletes one, permanently, with no recycle bin. Check what you're about to delete, and be extra careful in loops.

The next stage shows `pathlib`, a newer and often neater way to do all of this. You'll meet both in real code, so it's worth knowing the `os` way too.

challenges.promptMarkdown: Define `sort_by_extension(folder)` that moves every file in `folder` into a subfolder named after its extension without the dot (`txt`, `png`), creating the subfolders as needed. Files without an extension stay put. Return the number of files moved.
challenges.hint: For each file, `ext = os.path.splitext(name)[1][1:]`. Make `os.path.join(folder, ext)` and `os.rename` the file into it.
challenges.solution:
import os

def sort_by_extension(folder):
    moved = 0
    for name in os.listdir(folder):
        full = os.path.join(folder, name)
        ext = os.path.splitext(name)[1][1:]
        if not os.path.isfile(full) or not ext:
            continue
        target = os.path.join(folder, ext)
        os.makedirs(target, exist_ok=True)
        os.rename(full, os.path.join(target, name))
        moved += 1
    return moved

intro.title: Paths with pathlib
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`pathlib` is the modern way to work with paths. Instead of passing strings to `os` functions, you make a `Path` object, and the path itself knows how to answer questions about it. Many Python programmers prefer it, because the code reads naturally.

```
from pathlib import Path

p = Path("data") / "2026" / "sales.txt"   # / joins path parts
print(p)                  # data/2026/sales.txt (on Mac and Linux)
print(p.name)             # sales.txt
print(p.stem, p.suffix)   # sales .txt
print(p.parent)           # data/2026
```

The `/` operator joins parts, using the right separator for the computer, just like `os.path.join`. `.name` is the last part, `.stem` the name without its extension, `.suffix` the extension (with its dot) and `.parent` the folder above. Like `os.path`, these don't touch the disk.

Questions about the disk are methods: `p.exists()`, `p.is_file()` and `p.is_dir()`. `p.stat().st_size` is the size in bytes. `p.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` creates a folder and any missing ones above it.

For small files, a `Path` can read and write the whole text in one call, opening and closing the file for you: `p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")` returns the text, and `p.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")` replaces the file with it. For line-by-line work on big files, `p.open(encoding="utf-8")` works just like `open(p)`, with `with`.

```
from pathlib import Path

folder = Path("notes")
folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
(folder / "todo.txt").write_text("buy milk\n", encoding="utf-8")
print((folder / "todo.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
```

`folder.iterdir()` goes through everything in a folder, giving `Path` objects. `folder.glob("*.txt")` gives just the entries whose names match a pattern (`*` means "anything"), and `folder.rglob("*.txt")` also searches every folder inside it. Sort them when the order matters.

```
from pathlib import Path

for p in sorted(Path(".").glob("*.txt")):
    print(p.name, p.stat().st_size)
```

Anything that takes a path also takes a `Path`: `open(p)`, `os.path.exists(p)` and so on. Use `str(p)` when you really need it as text. `p.rename(new)` and `p.unlink()` (delete) work like `os.rename` and `os.remove`.

from pathlib import Path

def back_up(folder):
    count = 0
    for p in Path(folder).glob("*.txt"):
        p.with_name(p.name + ".bak").write_text(p.read_text(encoding="utf-8"), encoding="utf-8")
        count += 1
    return count

intro.title: When files go wrong
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Files live outside your program, so many things can go wrong that your code can't prevent: the file was moved or never existed, a folder sits where you expected a file, the disk is full, or you aren't allowed to read it. Each problem raises its own exception, and all of them are kinds of `OSError`:

```
OSError
├── FileNotFoundError     the file or folder doesn't exist
├── FileExistsError       it exists, but you needed it not to ("x" mode)
├── IsADirectoryError     you tried to open a folder as a file
├── NotADirectoryError    a file is in the way where a folder should be
└── PermissionError       you aren't allowed to read or write it
```

The usual pattern is `try` around the `with`, catching the specific problem you can do something about. A missing file is often a normal situation, such as the first time a program runs, before any save file exists:

```
def load_notes(name):
    try:
        with open(name, encoding="utf-8") as f:
            return f.read().splitlines()
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return []          # no notes yet: start empty

print(load_notes("no-notes-yet.txt"))   # []
```

The exception carries details: `e.filename` is the path involved, and `e.strerror` a description such as `No such file or directory`. Use them to give a clear message, such as `Can't find settings.txt`, rather than a traceback.

Catch `OSError` when any file problem should be handled the same way, such as "skip this file and carry on". Catch the narrow ones (`FileNotFoundError`) when only that problem is expected; let the others stop the program, so you hear about them.

Checking first with `os.path.exists` (LBYL) seems simpler, but the file could vanish between the check and the `open`, and it doesn't cover permissions or folders. Trying and catching (EAFP) handles every case at the moment it matters.

Reading a file with the wrong encoding raises `UnicodeDecodeError`, a kind of `ValueError` rather than `OSError`: the file opened fine, but its bytes don't make sense as text. The next stage explains bytes and encodings; for now, `open(..., errors="replace")` swaps unreadable bytes for a � instead of failing.

intro.title: Text, bytes and encodings
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Under the hood, every file is a sequence of **bytes**: numbers from 0 to 255. A text file is bytes that stand for characters, according to an **encoding**, a table that says which bytes mean which character. An image, a sound or a zip file is bytes with its own structure, which isn't text at all.

Python keeps the two apart. A `str` is text, made of characters; a `bytes` value is raw bytes, written with a `b` in front: `b"hi"`. `encode` turns text into bytes and `decode` turns bytes back into text, both using an encoding:

```
text = "café"
data = text.encode("utf-8")
print(data)                  # b'caf\xc3\xa9'
print(len(text), len(data))  # 4 5: the é takes two bytes
print(data.decode("utf-8"))  # café
```

**UTF-8** is the encoding almost everything uses today. It stores the plain English letters, digits and punctuation (the ASCII characters) as one byte each, and everything else, like é, ø, ж or 😀, as two to four bytes. That's why the number of characters and the number of bytes can differ.

Decoding with the wrong encoding gives garbled text (`cafÃ©`) or a `UnicodeDecodeError`. That's why you pass `encoding="utf-8"` to `open`: without it, Python uses the computer's default, which on some Windows machines is an older encoding, and the same program can read the same file differently on two computers.

For files that aren't text, open them in **binary mode** by adding `b` to the mode: `"rb"` or `"wb"`. Then `read()` returns `bytes` and `write()` takes `bytes`, with no encoding and no line-break translation. Indexing a `bytes` value gives a number: `b"ABC"[0]` is `65`.

```
with open("tiny.bin", "wb") as f:
    f.write(bytes([0, 1, 2, 255]))

with open("tiny.bin", "rb") as f:
    data = f.read()
print(data, list(data), len(data))   # b'\x00\x01\x02\xff' [0, 1, 2, 255] 4
```

Many file types start with a fixed **signature**, a few bytes that identify them: every PNG image starts with `b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n"`, and every zip file with `b"PK"`. Reading the first few bytes in binary mode is how programs recognise a file whatever its name says.

Big binary files, like videos, are best copied in **chunks**: `f.read(65536)` reads up to 64 KB at a time, and a loop continues until `read` returns `b""`, so the whole file never has to fit in memory.

intro.title: Processing text files
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Most real file work follows one pattern: **read** some input, **process** it, and **write** the result somewhere else. Filtering a log for errors, renaming a word throughout a document, totalling a list of sales: all are the same three steps, with different processing in the middle.

```
with open("app.log", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("INFO start\nERROR disk full\nINFO saved\nERROR timeout\n")

with open("app.log", encoding="utf-8") as src, open("errors.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as dst:
    for line in src:
        if line.startswith("ERROR"):
            dst.write(line)

with open("errors.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())   # just the two ERROR lines
```

Opening the input and the output in one `with` and working line by line means even a huge log never has to fit in memory: each line is read, checked and written before the next one is read. Lines that are written unchanged keep their own `\n`, so no extra line breaks are needed.

When the processing needs the **whole** input first, such as sorting, counting or finding the top values, read everything (or build a dict as you go), then write the result in a second step. Keep the steps in separate functions, `load`, `summarise` and `save`, and each one is easy to test on its own.

**Write to a new file**, never back into the one you're reading. If the program fails halfway, the original is still there. When the result really must replace the original, write it to a temporary name and then swap it into place with `os.replace(temp, original)`, which replaces the file in one step, so there's never a moment with a half-written file.

```
import os

def replace_word(name, old, new):
    with open(name, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        text = f.read()
    temp = name + ".tmp"
    with open(temp, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(text.replace(old, new))
    os.replace(temp, name)     # swap in the finished file
```

Processing often combines several files (merging monthly reports into one) or splits one into several (one output file per category). The patterns are the same; only the number of `open` calls changes. A dict of open files, or a dict of lists written out at the end, keeps the splitting tidy.

challenges.solution:
def clean(src, dst):
    seen = set()
    written = 0
    with open(src, encoding="utf-8") as fin, open(dst, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fout:
        for line in fin:
            line = line.strip()
            if not line or line.startswith("#") or line in seen:
                continue
            seen.add(line)
            fout.write(line + "\n")
            written += 1
    return written

challenges.title: Expert: Run the commands
challenges.promptMarkdown: Define `run(name, commands)`: load the list, carry out each command (`add <task>` replies `Added: <task>`; `done <n>` replies `Done: <task>` or `No task <n>`; `list` gives the `show` lines; `clear` removes finished tasks and replies `Cleared <count>`; anything else `Unknown command`), save the list, and return all the replies.
challenges.hint: Split each command with `partition(" ")`. For `done`, convert the number and index the list inside `try`, catching `ValueError` and `IndexError` (and treat numbers below 1 as missing).

tests.label: The lesson example
tests.assertion: run("todo.txt", ["add pay rent", "done 2", "clear", "list"]) == ["Added: pay rent", "Done: call Ana", "Cleared 2", "1. [ ] water the plants", "2. [ ] pay rent"]

tests.label: Bad commands
tests.assertion: run("t5.txt", ["done 9", "done x", "done 0", "dance", "list"]) == ["No task 9", "No task x", "No task 0", "Unknown command", "Nothing to do!"]

questions.prompt: Why store the tasks as `[x] title` lines?

choices.label: It is easy for both the program and a person to read

questions.explanation: A simple text format can be read by the program and edited by a person.

questions.prompt: What should `load` return the very first time, before the file exists?

choices.label: A list with one empty task

questions.explanation: No file yet means no tasks yet.

questions.prompt: Why does `save` write to a `.tmp` file first?

choices.label: So a crash mid-save can never leave a half-written list

questions.explanation: Writing to a temp file and then renaming it means the real file is always complete.

questions.prompt: What does `"[ ] call Ana"[4:]` give?
questions.explanation: The status takes the first 4 characters (`[ ] `), so the title starts at index 4.

questions.prompt: `clear` removes the finished tasks. With 2 of 5 tasks done, how many are left? (a number)
questions.explanation: Removing the 2 finished tasks leaves 3.

questions.prompt: Why catch `IndexError` for `done 9`?

choices.label: There is no task 9, and the program should reply instead of crashing

questions.explanation: A bad task number is a normal mistake, so catch it and reply with a helpful message.
